Hirschsprung's disease is a congenital disorder in which nerve cells that help the large intestine contract are absent. This usually affects the lower part of the intestine (the rectum). In some cases it may also affect other parts of the GI tract including the small intestine or stomach. The condition causes severe constipation and swelling of the belly. This is an emergency scenario. The patient is in shock from their trauma but is still hypoperfusing tissues at a rate that is sufficient to keep the brain alive. Therefore they are in shock with impaired consciousness (ICS). ICS is defined as when the patient has a blood pressure less than 90mmHg or a systolic blood pressure more than 20% below the patients previous blood pressure and has either disorganised respiratory patterns, significant limp muscle tone or both. In this situation intubation must be performed before any other treatment. If the patient was just in shock without ICS then you would perform a cricothyrotomy. Cardioversion would be used for an atrial fibrillation patient who was haemodynamically stable. A CT scan may be useful to evaluate the extent of the traumatic injury but is unlikely to be the best initial option. A tracheotomy is a last resort procedure that would only be considered if you've tried everything else and the patient is still failing to oxygenate. Source - Acute medicine lecture. Case 14. In this case, caffeine is acting as a stimulant (by binding to adenosine receptors) which will prevent drowsiness. During waking hours, adenosine builds up in the brain. Adenosine then switches on sleep pressure by binding to adenosine receptors. This slows down the activity of the brain. When we go to sleep, adenosine is broken down into inactive compounds (such as adenosine monophosphate). This is done via glycogenic pathways (stored as glycogen). At night when we are asleep, glycogen is released back into glucose by the action of glucagon. Therefore, if there was no adenosine breakdown during the day, sleep would never occur at night. Addison's disease is a chronic endocrine disorder caused by inadequate secretions of adrenal cortex hormones. It is usually primary (idiopathic) but may be secondary to other diseases. Symptoms develop slowly over months or years and include fatigue, nausea, dizziness, and weight loss. Darkening of the skin in persons of any race (hyperpigmentation) and hyperkalemia are common. Other findings may include hypotension, muscle pain, and dehydration. Addison's disease should be suspected in patients who have these symptoms and signs and who have a history of recent stress such as infection, injury, or surgery. Diagnosis is based on low levels of cortisol and aldosterone. Treatment consists of glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.  The adrenal glands lie above the kidneys and produce more than 50 different hormones, including adrenaline and cortisol. Adrenal insufficiency occurs when the adrenal glands don’t make enough of these hormones. If the problem is only with making cortisol, it’s called primary adrenal insufficiency, or Addison’s disease. If it’s also a problem making adrenaline, it’s called secondary adrenal insufficiency. Addison’s disease is rare. It affects about one in 100,000 people in the UK. It can develop at any age, but most commonly starts between 30 and 50 years old. It’s two to four times more common in women than men. The cause of Addison’s disease is damage to the adrenal glands. Hair cells release glutamate when depolarised, and release ATP when hyperpolarised. Spiral ganglion cells release ATP when depolarised and release GABA when hyperpolarised. The inner ear has a special role in maintaining balance. The brain expects the fluid in the semicircular ducts to move at approximately 1 degree per second in the same direction as the head is moving. Vertical movement of the head causes fluid in the semicircular ducts to move. This deflects hair cells towards the vestibule, so that their ciliated processes bend away from the vestibule. This decreases the release rate of ATP, and increases the release rate of glutamate. The brain interprets this as a decrease in speed, and compensates by turning the head in the opposite direction. Head tilting causes horizontal rotation of the fluid in semicercular ducts. This causes hair cells to be deflected towards the vestibule, so that their ciliated processes bend away from the vestibule. This decreases the release rate of glutamate, and increases the release rate of ATP. The brain interprets this as a change in direction, and compensates by turning the head in the same direction. Pagets disease of bone is a condition in which abnormal bone growth makes your bones more likely to fracture. Symptoms include:Tiredness and general weaknessPain in the spine or hipPainful fractures that occur out of nowhere. These may be caused by something as simple as a cough or a fall.Swelling of the legs or ribs due to the pressure of abnormal bone growth.The fractures that people with Pagets experience tend to happen without any injury or stress. Some common sites of fracture include the pelvis, spine, femur, tibia, humerus, radius, clavicle and ribs.These fractures often occur after only minor trauma such as a fall from standing height or less, or a bump from playing sport.In some cases, the pain is worse at night and gets better during the day. Treatment involves treating the symptoms and preventing further complications. This includes reducing the amount of weight bearing through the affected areas, and surgery to remove the damaged sections of bone. This does not cure the condition but it can relieve pain and improve mobility. A type of drug called bisphosphonates can also help reduce bone pain and prevent fractures. Other treatments may include:exercises to strengthen muscles around the joints painkillers to treat bone pain a walking stick or other aid if you’re unsteady on your feet compression stockings to prevent swelling in your legs and feet supportive shoes to relieve foot pain a brace to support the spine if this is affected massage to relieve muscle tension physiotherapy to improve movement and flexibility a special diet if you develop kidney stones. Pagets disease is thought to result from a combination of genetic and environmental factors. It usually affects men over 50, although it can occur in younger people and women. Its not clear exactly how many people have it, but estimates suggest up to 1 in every 200 people over the age of 50 may have the condition. Closure of the foramen ovale: After the first breath has been taken, oxygen enters the alveoli for the first time and it signals the arterioles to dilate. Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with amiodarone use. It has a characteristic ECG shape. The other medications listed are also drugs that have an effect on the electrophysiology of the heart but they do not produce the specific ECG changes seen in TdP.  The treatment of TdP involves stopping the offending agent if it is known or withdrawal of other QT prolonging drugs. If this fails then overdrive pacing, intravenous infusion of magnesium sulphate or procainamide may be used to restore sinus rhythm.  Ventricular tachycardia is a rapid regular rhythem of the ventricles. It is characterised by a QRS duration >0.4 seconds and a heart rate >100 bpm. VT can be haemodynamically unstable and can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. The treatment of VT depends on the nature of the arrhythmia. If it is non-haemodynamic then vagal manoeuvres such as breath holding or carotid sinus massage maybe used to terminate the arrhythmia. If this fails then defibrillation with synchronised cardioversion may be needed.  Haemodynamically stable VT can be treated using pharmacological measures, such as IV adenosine or verapamil, or electrical cardioversion. If the VT is haemodynamically unstable then defibrillation with synchronised cardioversion is required.   Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a distinct form of ventricular tachycardia due to early after depolarisations (EADs). Typically it occurs during exercise and is self limiting. Treatment is usually observation only.  Source: Dr Coffey's lecture on Cardiac Arrhythmias from Case 13 and the Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine.
